I'm not quite sure what you're saying. Do you mean you don't think it's
legal to base future game behavior on past game experience with another
player because it's considered an "out of game" consideration or that you
don't think it's reasonable to do so?

If the former, I'm not sure whether you're right in a technical sense or
not but I'm pretty sure that if it is illegal, such an interpretation of
that rule is entirely unenforcable. When we sit down with other players
we've played with before, we know all kinds of things about them: what
clans they like to play, whether they play combat or vote or bleed well
or poorly. And whether they break deals capriciously, occasionally, or
never. It would be stupid not to use such knowledge as you play the
game and no one tries to ignore it. Therefore, if this _were_ the rule,
we all play illegally all the time.

If the latter, I disagree. Knowing how a player views past deals he makes
as the game continues is very important information and even one experience
with another player will tell me a lot of useful information. Whether I
believe a third party's opinion - on the other hand - is another matter.

Fred

In message <1127800811....@z14g2000cwz.googlegroups.com>, Daley

<dal...@iinet.net.au> writes:
>Correct me if I am wrong... but isnt it illegal to carry over the
>effects (ie. deal breaking) from one game to the next?

It is impossible to prevent players from carrying knowledge of players'
behaviour from game to game, tournament to tournament. The rules never
force you to accept a deal and you are perfectly entitled to tell
someone "No, because you'll stab me in the back, like you did back in
1922." Similarly, you could say to someone "No, I don't think you have
the skill to pull that off, but I'd have to do all my work first and it
would be wasted, so no deal" - bringing knowledge of your experience of
a player's skill to a decision.

It is, however, illegal to violate play to win based on something like,
for example, "OH MY GOD HE'S A DEAL BREAKER I HAVE TO OUST HIM RIGHT NOW

You'd think no one had heard of the Prisoners' Dilemma. Depending on
the payout matrix, backstabs that pay off bigger than cooperating may
result in a lower long-term profit if mutual distrust pays off less
than either.

Since no one can claim to have done a payout analysis for this game,
people who insist that breaking deals is smarter than keeping them are
just expressing their personal preference, as are people whose strategy
is to keep them. Since the short-term benefits of the backstab are
always so strong and so immediate, I suspect many have trouble
recognizing the long-term benefits--it's like smoking crack versus not
smoking crack. In the short term, I understand crack is pretty darn
good. :)

But there's another undercurrent in this whole discussion: it's
obviously in the interest of habitual dealbreakers to keep habitual
dealkeepers from trusting each other. Take all this "pinhead" yapping
with a grain of salt.

Unlike the classic prisoner's dilemma, though, you aren't always being
offered the same deal and you aren't always aware of being backstabbed.

From the first point: I might back out on a big deal when I suddenly see
a chance to sweep (my one Pulse of the Canaille turns up and I check
everyone's hand, in some fantasy scenario). This might screw up my
credibility for BIG BIG BIG deals, but it's quite possible that some
players will think "Yeah, I can trust him for a little deal."

I can also offer deals where I go first. Unlike the Prisoner's Dilemma,
things aren't simultaneous. Think I'll backstab you? Okay. I'll rush
Arika now on the condition that you don't bleed me next turn. I go
first. You can't get burned. (This will help restore any wounds in my
credibility, too!)

On the second point: I say "You give me 2 pool from that Parity Shift,
I'll Rush Sweaty Nash and I reckon I can put him in torpor." Okay! You
give me 2 pool. I rush Sweaty. I play Carrion Crows. I play Quick
Meld in response to a Fake Out. I play Claws of the Dead. I play
Scorpion Sting. Sweaty plays Majesty. Darn, I say, I don't have any
Psyche!s to hand now. Goshdarnit. Isn't that a pity?

Have I just backstabbed you? It might well be worth me cycling my ahnd
and getting two pool, but not worth torporising Sweaty because I reckon
I can do something more interesting with him. Or I might not have any
Psyche!s in my hand.

Well, both at various points in this thread. But the interesting ones
to discuss are the ones for which the payoff to break must be at least
as greater and likely greater than any possible result the player gets
if he upholds the deal. For example:

Player A has Jost Werner with 1 blood, 1 pool, and no library cards. His
prey is player B.

Player B has Arika with 1 blood, 1 pool, and one Kine Resources Contested
card in hand, no other library cards. His prey is player C.

Player C has Muaziz with 1 blood, 3 pool, no library cards, and 1 victory
point. His prey is (now) player A.

It's player A's turn. He is expecting to take his one sure victory point
when player B interrupts him and offers to call Kine Resources contested,
putting 3 points on C and one point on himself.

If you're player A, do you take the deal?

If you're player B and player A takes the deal, do you go through with it
or do you double-cross player A?

To resolve the issue, bypass player A's dilemma for the time being and let
him look at the issue from player B's perspective. Player B only goes
through with the deal if he cares more about his reputation in the long run
than if he wants the game win. Knowing that, player A only _possibly_
trusts player B if player B actually has some kind of a reputation to
protect. If player B has been in this position before and succumbed to
temptation, there's no reason to think he wouldn't likewise succumb now.
(Maybe the only argument player B could make is if the prior time, the
stakes were higher: that was for large tournament win; this is just a
preliminary round in a small tournament. I don't know. It would take a
massive difference to convince me.)

This has a bunch of philosophical, "Why-do-you-game?" type implications.
And quite arguably, if the deal is offered, accepted, and kept in the
end, charges of metagaming would be hard to deny. If metagaming, why
would the deal not be considered an out-of-game consideration and thus
illegal? And, if it were illegal, would it likewise be illegal if the
offer was made, accepted, but not kept (backstabbed). Would it illegal
to even make the offer?

Fred

cards is playing the game, but tabletalk and dealmaking/breaking
is player character.

confined to the cards/rules, then I challenge you to distinguish
why *this* aspect of the game is treated differently than, say,
using brute force, bribes, breaking the rules, etc. (other

the banal "I play a kray-Z MaLkaViaN, so I can just do whatever

the effects generated by clan-specific cards, that is), I do not
see why playing a deceptive methuselah would be legal in-game
reason enough to lie, dealbreak, etc. as a player.

To get back to your actor example: deception through cards is
like an actor lying in character in a movie. Lying as a player
at the table would be like the actor lying about a role he plays,
say, to fellow actors. The former is no reason to assume the
person is a lying cheat; the latter can well be.

I can understand the use of extreme examples to point out a situation.
But then again, let's get roleplaying as an example. Per your logic,
anyone playing a Vampire RPG game is inherently capable of drinking
real blood or the like.

The point of the RPG is exactly to "play" (in the acting sense)
something you wouldn't be, or "do" in a fantasy way something you
wouldn't do. It is often refereed as a powerful tool to understand how
certain types of people feel about their condition, or to understand
why certain people act this or that way. I believe that it is also a
great tool for anyone to test its own personal mettle regarding ethics
- when you play a theft in a healthy RPG environment, you're not prone
to repeat your character's actions in real life, you just get an
insight of a thief's motives and mind to make a *really* conscious
choice to NOT practice theft in real life. If one cannot grasp that,
one simply discovered its morality was not so firm as one would
believe.

Though cardgames are not roleplaying games, they're based (at least
most of them) on RPG fantasy settings, and I simply don't believe
there's any reason for CCG players to play them in an acting sense.
It's not that every VTES player should play the part and dress like a
vampire and so what - even most RPG players don't go that far - but the
game was built around a setting that includes stories of backstabbing,
intrigue and politics. So why drive out backstabbing in the game
context? Why push that beyond the table situation? Why don't actors who
played serial killers in movies don't come around killing people in
real life?

About drawing the line: everyone draws the line where they feel it's
right to draw it - but that does not mean you can safely conclude that
some *will* draw the line further to a point where you wouldn't accept
it. Some will undoubtely act in real life as they act when breaking
deals, sure. But most stable and socially aware people will draw the
line where the game ends and real life begins - so there's no point in
trying to condemn in-game dealbreaking as a extension of real-world
stances. It's basically the same as condenming a pro-abortion person as
a potential murderer, so everyone should stand against abortion. That
view on abortion had to do with that topic alone, it's not like one'll
support it out of a larger disregard for social standards (i.e., not
killing equals).

to do that out of the game". It most certainly include people that take
the stance that "doing this in game means no harm to anyone and it's
part of the fun, so why shouldn't I? I don't do this in real world to
anyone anyway". It also include "i'm just playing a part, like an
actor" people. In fact, most players (and I mean MOST) probably can dig
that easily.

You're free to conclude that one or other dealbreaker is prone to
backstab you out of game too. Of course you are. But once you bring it
at a debate, it gets a whole new, generalizing context, when it should
come by in a personal level only - i.e., you assess each people you
know in person and conclude how far they'd go with the backstabbing
thing. Undoubtely you'll know some that you can't lend a single dime
to, and others that you can trust your life with. But using your best
judgement to extend that option to any dealbreaker or to the
possibilities the game present in that camp is a stretch at best.

Children play games of police and thieves. They need no card, rules, or

coming together to get fun). They not even need anything resembling the

"suspects" of this "heinous crime" as the others.

adulthood malice - as adults in a healthy social environment, we should
be even more aware of the moral implications of *real* thefting and

to play the part as the children do? That's absurd. Or just because
some people made the conscious choice of ignoring the implications and
live with the consequences? It's almost an offense to our capacity as
grown-up people to expect we *need* these tools to separate things.

each people you know according how they act. It's not that transposing
in-game behaviour to out-of-game ethics is a good start. More often

Speaking falsehood, breaking one's word, and misleading others
are against social values in just about any part of the world.
It makes no difference if you conjecture a place where they've
codified such social mores into law. The legal status isn't the
issue. The issue is whether the context of these things is taken
into account. Most people seem to have an innate understanding
that doing such things in the context of a mere game does not
constitute the sort of problem which makes them an anathema in
real life. Presumedly, that would be just as true in Pinheadia
as anywhere else. However, if no such distinction is made in
Pinheadia law, then the answer is that by law, VtES could not
be played in Pinheadia in the same manner as it were elsewhere.

If Pinheadia law likewise proscribed sporting events which
lasted more than two hours, then many American sports couldn't
be played the same way they are elsewhere since the length of
the game is a key element in its play. So what? What is the
point of this analogy? It seems to ignore the critical issues
in considering whether lying in the context of a game is
morally different than lying in the context of other
activities.

Concerning the comparison with violence, most people, regardless
of where they are, understand that unchecked violence is
generally harmful to civilized society. Hence, it is not a
coincidental thing that radically liberal laws about free use
of fisticuffs does not exist anywhere in the civilized world
(at least, not that I've heard of). There may be some specific
exceptions of various types in various places, but the idea
that overall it's a bad thing seems to be universal. By contrast
(again), the notion that my card "attacks" your card in a game
and "beats it up" is usually just fine. Same thing: game violence
doesn't actually hurt anything any more than game lying and game
deal-breaking.

Fred
